On one NVIDIA H100 GPU, with Haar-random interferometers, twice as many modes as photonic inputs and photon-number-resolving detectors, the frontier lies at 38.3 single photons and at 31.0 entangled photons from one emitter. For squeezed light, a timing model fitted to measurements places it at 41.5 squeezed photonic inputs of mean photon number 0.5. For our samplers, coherence alone makes simulation harder: sources that emit a photon with probability one half reach 64.2 when vacuum and photon are mixed incoherently, as for lossy single photons, but only 50.0 when they are in coherent superposition. Feed-forward from mid-circuit measurement of up to three modes lowers the single-photon frontier only from 38.3 to 38.1.
2611.12876.why: Defines the simulability frontier as one exact classical sample per second and recomputes it across photonic light types.

eli5.plain: Proposes a common yardstick for when photonic devices outrun classical computers.
eli5.how: Time to draw one exact sample on a fixed machine; doubling hardware speed moves the frontier by about one photon.
eli5.matters: Clarifies quantum-advantage claims, relevant to bosonic sampling with microwave modes.
eli5.caveat: The metric favours exactness; practical advantage often concerns approximate sampling.

2611.16595.title: Gatemon qubits based on in-situ ternary InAsSb/Al nanowire Josephson junctions
2611.16595.abstract: Ternary InAsSb/Al nanowires combine compositionally engineerable semiconductor properties with epitaxial proximity superconductivity, making them attractive for hybrid quantum circuits and mesoscopic superconductivity. Here, we realize gatemon qubits based on shadow-defined in-situ InAsSb/Al Josephson junctions in a single growth process. Gate-dependent microwave spectroscopy demonstrates electrostatic tuning of the qubit transition over several gigahertz. Rabi oscillations and Ramsey interference show coherent qubit control, with representative values T1 = 0.79 us and T2* = 0.91 us. Across five gatemons distributed over three chips, the measured relaxation times range from approximately 0.2 us to 1 us and decrease with increasing qubit frequency. Their magnitude is comparable to a circuit estimate of spontaneous emission into the electromagnetic environment. These results establish in-situ InAsSb/Al junctions as coherent, gate-tunable circuit elements and introduce cQED architecture as a microwave probe of the dynamics of the ternary weak link.
2611.16595.why: Gatemons from in-situ InAsSb/Al nanowires tune over GHz but reach only sub-microsecond T1.

2611.13157.title: Mimicking the zero-field Josephson diode effect with remanent magnetization and self-field
2611.13157.abstract: A Josephson junction whose critical current is larger in one direction than in the other is a diode. With a magnetized barrier, a junction can be a diode at zero applied field, and this is commonly attributed to an intrinsic Josephson diode effect, in which the magnetic barrier breaks time-reversal symmetry. Here we show that the same signatures arise from two ordinary ingredients: the magnetic field of the bias current in the electrodes and the remanent magnetization of the barrier. In cross-type Nb/Pd$_{89}$Ni$_{11}$/Nb junctions, the self-field displaces the interference patterns of the two current polarities in opposite directions. An in-plane remanent magnetization translates the pattern and brings the resulting asymmetry to zero field, where the junction mimics a nonvolatile diode with an asymmetry of 10 to 12% and a polarity set by the magnetization direction. Reversing the current or the field cannot distinguish this mimic from an intrinsic effect, but the wiring can: moving the current lead to the other arm of the electrode across the field reverses the self-field diode, in applied field and at zero field alike, whereas an intrinsic diode would be unchanged. This gives a simple dc test for Josephson diodes in the current-perpendicular-to-plane geometry.
2611.13157.why: Zero-field Josephson diode behaviour in Nb/PdNi/Nb junctions comes from self-field and remanent magnetization, not intrinsic symmetry breaking.

2611.11044.title: Exact sampling beyond Fock inputs and linear optics: photon-number superpositions, photonic matrix-product states, adaptive and non-linear circuits
2611.11044.abstract: Clifford and Clifford's algorithm samples single-photon boson sampling exactly, one output mode at a time, by adding the input photons in a uniformly random order. We extend this construction to other input states and to adaptive and non-linear circuits. It applies whenever non-negative weights on output prefixes and input sets satisfy one marginal identity, a set-chain lemma: the random-order sampler is then exact at one weight evaluation per candidate mode, and it gives the posterior over the hidden input set. We build four exact samplers on it. For sources in a superposition of vacuum and one photon, the weights are rectangular permanents on an offset input set, and the cost has the exponent of single photons under loss. For photonic matrix-product states of bond dimension $χ$, a gap-by-gap Kraus contraction turns each weight into a short sum of squared amplitudes. For adaptive linear optics, the chain starts from the posterior given the adaptive counts and rejects chains that contradict them. For a single-mode non-linear phase the identity fails, and rejection from linear branches is exact with acceptance $1/\|c\|_1^2$. All four samplers agree with strong simulation on small instances, and cost models put adaptive sampling with up to three adaptive modes within $10\%$ of single photons and a non-linear site at $\varphi=π/2$ at about $4\times$.
2611.11044.why: Extends Clifford–Clifford exact boson sampling to photon-number superpositions, MPS inputs and adaptive circuits.

2611.14114.title: Cross-Platform Benchmarking of GHZ-State Generation in Quantum Processors via Cloud Services
2611.14114.abstract: Quantum computing has rapidly evolved into a diverse ecosystem of hardware platforms that differ in their underlying technologies and operational characteristics. Consequently, benchmarking has become essential for identifying the strengths of quantum processors, comparing their performance, and enabling informed decisions when selecting the most appropriate quantum computing platform for specific applications. In this work, we benchmark nine commercially accessible quantum processors from five vendors, spanning superconducting and trapped-ion technologies, using the multipartite entanglement benchmark from the QuSquare suite. All experiments were performed through remote cloud-access services, with the default compilation of each provider and without error mitigation, reflecting the performance experienced by end users. The benchmark estimates the fidelity of Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) states by direct fidelity estimation and searches for the largest GHZ state whose fidelity is compatible, within the statistical error, with the genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) threshold $F=1/2$. Our results reveal a substantial gap between the total number of physical qubits available on a processor and the size of the largest GHZ state passing the benchmark: the best superconducting processors reach $N^*=27$ and $N^*=24$ qubits, less than a quarter of their registers, whereas the 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes with its full register. We further show that median calibration data are poor predictors of the benchmark outcome, and that the reported sizes depend strongly on the statistical decision rule: requiring certified GME reduces the number of devices that succeed at any tested size from nine to four. These results provide a baseline for future cross-platform benchmarking of quantum processors.
2611.14114.why: Benchmarks GHZ fidelity on nine cloud processors from five vendors with default compilation.

2611.12280.title: Calibration-free quantum thermometry with strain-swept two-level defects
2611.12280.abstract: Superconducting qubits operate within a well-defined temperature range, making local temperature monitoring important. Here we show that intrinsic two-level defects in Josephson-junction barriers can act as local thermometers by exploiting the shape of their population response, without requiring calibration of the readout offset or contrast. Marginalizing over these unknown parameters imposes an identifiability requirement absent from single-parameter thermometric bounds: for narrow sweeps, usable information scales as the fourth power of the sweep width. Hence, a narrow sweep becomes locally indistinguishable from a change in offset or contrast. We illustrate this principle with a strain-swept two-level defect in a Josephson junction. For a reported defect with tunneling energy $Δ_{0}/h=\SI{1.3}{\giga\hertz}$, swept along one branch of its hyperbola to \SI{2.69}{\giga\hertz} (an asymmetry excursion of \SI{2.36}{\giga\hertz}, or \SI{8}{\volt} of piezo voltage), the analysis projects a single-defect fit precision of \SI{0.58}{\percent} at \SI{20}{\milli\kelvin}. The resulting response enables temperature estimation without prior calibration of the readout offset and contrast, while the same sweep overdetermines the Boltzmann form and identifies significant deviations from thermality. These results establish intrinsic junction defects as a resource for calibration-free local thermometry and highlight identifiability as a key design criterion for primary temperature sensing.
2611.12280.why: Strain-swept junction TLS can act as calibration-free thermometers, but narrow sweeps lose information as the fourth power of width.

2611.13221.title: Exceptional points in non-Markovian quantum-state diffusion: From coefficient dynamics to state signatures
2611.13221.abstract: An exceptional point of a memory-coefficient equation need not have the same signature in every quantum-state observable. We examine this relation within exact non-Markovian quantum-state diffusion (NMQSD), following the same operator closure from its coefficient dynamics to the non-Markovian master equation obtained by noise averaging. A finite homogeneous lift identifies the Jordan chains reached by the causal initialization, while state reconstruction determines which contributions survive in a specified readout. Two models expose the distinction. For common-bath qubits restricted to zero and one excitation, a noise-independent lowering-form $O$ operator gives a closed master equation. Every defective decaying mode transfers its full pole order to a suitable unconditional excitation--reference coherence. A known third-order configuration illustrates both a quadratic--exponential coherence and cancellation of its highest-order term in another quadrature. For a position-coupled oscillator in a fixed-photon-number optomechanical sector, the exact closure contains a scalar noise-history term. On the regular normalizable branch studied for bath decay rates below the oscillator frequency, two second-order coefficient blocks lead to a double pole in the conditional displacement response to the NMQSD noise history, at long preparation age and fixed lag. The purely algebraic coefficient tail cancels from the conditional Gaussian width. Complete noise averaging changes the master-equation coefficients and combines conditional width with the weighted spread of state centers. Together, the models show how causal preparation, state reconstruction, and averaging give coefficient exceptional points a precise, readout-dependent meaning.
2611.13221.why: Shows exceptional points in non-Markovian quantum-state-diffusion coefficients need not appear in every observable.

2611.18278.title: Observing Enhanced Entanglement in an Ising Quantum Register Beyond Weak Measurement
2611.18278.abstract: Measurements often yield a disentangled quantum state which is the most probable measurement outcome while the measurement outcomes with enhanced entanglement could be exponentially less probable or absent. Higher probability in measurement outcomes with enhanced entanglement is virtue in experimental observation of enhance entanglement in post-selected or Born-rule measurements with less resources in noisy quantum devices. We develop a periodic measurement sampling(PMS) protocol in the framework of uniform matrix product states. Using PMS, we identify a peak enhancement of entanglement in a uniform post-measurement state whose probabilistic outcome can be maximized by optimizing a measurement super-cell. A measurement super-cell is the smallest repeating building block of qubits defined by the measurement density, external field strength and exchange interactions between quantum register and ancilla qubits. The above prediction based on a classical description of the many-body quantum state is demonstrated in a quantum computing experiment in a loop of quantum register qubits with Ising interactions in the presence of transverse magnetic field. Further, we show the scalability of predictions of the periodic measurement sampling protocol in the thermodynamic limit to finite size systems. Especially, we present a rescaling ansatz which would enable predicting the possibility of observing enhanced entanglement in finite size systems.
2611.18278.why: Periodic measurement sampling with optimised super-cells raises the probability of entanglement-enhanced post-measurement states.

eli5.plain: A recipe to choose which qubits to measure so that the rare outcomes with more entanglement become common.
eli5.how: Uniform matrix-product states identify measurement super-cells that maximise both enhancement and its probability.
eli5.matters: Relevant to measurement-induced entanglement on noisy devices.
eli5.caveat: Resource-oriented rather than foundational.

2611.15416.title: Extractable Work from Collective Dark-State Charging of Quantum Batteries
2611.15416.abstract: We consider two ensembles of superconducting qubits coupled to a common lossy resonator, one serving as the charger and the other the battery. Destructive interference between their collective decay amplitudes selects a tunable family of many-body dark states, allowing controlled excitation transfer from the charger to the battery. The collective charging dynamics preserves the symmetric Dicke subspace of the battery, so its reduced state has at most $N+1$ nonzero eigenvalues. Together with the $N$-fold degeneracy of the battery's first excited energy level, this restriction keeps the passive energy of the entire battery below the single-qubit excitation energy $ω_0$, independently of the battery size. When the average stored energy per battery qubit is fixed and nonzero, the total stored energy grows linearly with $N$, while the ratio of global ergotropy to stored energy approaches unity as $N$ increases.
2611.15416.why: Collective dark-state charging of a qubit-ensemble 'battery' through a shared lossy resonator caps passive energy below one quantum.

eli5.plain: A theory of storing energy in many superconducting qubits via shared, interference-protected decay into a resonator.
eli5.how: Destructive interference of collective decay picks dark states that move excitations from charger to battery while staying in the symmetric subspace.
eli5.matters: Collective dark states in a shared lossy mode are standard waveguide/cavity-QED tools; the paper applies them to work extraction.
eli5.caveat: Quantum-battery framing; no experiment, and the collective coupling assumes identical qubits.

2611.10351.title: Realizing Unstructured PDE Forecasting on Superconducting Quantum Processors
2611.10351.abstract: Simulating high dimensional unstructured Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) with quantum processors is a major challenge with significant potential benefit. Existing methods have been demonstrated at small qubit counts, on simplifications of realistic problems. We implement a quantum reservoir network (QRN) for forecasting high-dimensional unstructured PDEs using up to 52 qubits on IBM superconducting hardware. Our method is gradient-free and does not suffer from the challenges of variational quantum algorithms. Instead, the QRN provides a large kernel space, up to 2^52 dimensions and beyond the reach of exact classical simulation, that remains useful under current hardware noise levels. Furthermore, a partial measure-and-reset mechanism enables total circuit runtime for ~24 times the qubit coherence time, so qubit lifetimes do not limit the forecast horizon. Thus, our method enables forecasting realistic unstructured nonlinear PDEs on quantum hardware. Typical difficulties associated with predicting large scale PDEs, such as transpilation, exponential shot requirements, hardware noise, and short qubit lifetimes are mitigated through careful design considerations and a dynamic observable reconstruction method. We validate our approach using a ~34k cell unstructured 2D cylinder flow at Reynolds number 1000 and a challenging nonlinear Gray--Scott reaction--diffusion problem, demonstrating high fidelity prediction on CUDA-Q simulation and on 26 and 52-qubit superconducting quantum processors. Specifically, we show that adding QRN features to an autoencoder linear prediction pipeline reduces prediction error by 21%-43%. Finally, we demonstrate closed-loop autoregressive PDE forecasting on these problems. This work demonstrates, for the first time, quantum circuits with depth beyond qubit lifetimes achieving accurate unstructured mesh forecasting on highly nonlinear PDEs.
2611.10351.why: Quantum reservoir network on up to 52 IBM qubits forecasts unstructured PDEs with mid-circuit reset extending runtime.

2611.10500.title: On the estimation of linear-optical amplitudes and probabilities with entangled input state
2611.10500.abstract: Most proposed applications of boson samplers, including photonic machine-learning models, do not use the samples themselves but estimates of output probabilities, marginals or overlaps, obtained to additive precision from a finite number of shots. For product inputs such as single photons, these quantities can already be estimated classically with Gurvits's algorithm and its generalisations. We ask whether entangled inputs change this picture. For any $n$-photon input that is a matrix-product state of bond dimension $χ$, with one photon per site and $L$ modes per site, we give an unbiased estimator of any output amplitude of an $m$-mode interferometer, whose mean-square error after $N$ draws is at most $\|ψ\|^2/N$ whatever the interferometer, the output pattern and the entanglement of the state. Each draw costs $O(nLχ^2+nL^3+mn)$ operations after $O(nLχ^3)$ preprocessing, and an additive error $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-δ$ requires $O(\|ψ\|^2\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/δ))$ draws, with memory of the order of the input size. The main application is to light emitted sequentially by quantum emitters, such as spin-based sources of photonic cluster states, for which $χ$ is bounded by the dimension of the source's retained quantum memory: one spin gives $χ=2$ at any length, and a memory of $k$ qubits, held in emitters or in photons stored in a delay line, gives $χ\le2^k$, so the cost stays polynomial as long as $k=O(\log n)$. The same sampler also estimates traced-memory probabilities, overlaps and individual marginal probabilities. All guarantees are additive: the estimator gives neither relative estimates of exponentially small probabilities nor a sampler of the output distribution.
2611.10500.why: Unbiased estimator of linear-optical amplitudes for MPS-entangled inputs with bounded variance.

2611.14629.title: Quantum Computing Enhanced Search for Wavelike Dark Matter
2611.14629.abstract: Identifying a weak, stochastic signal hidden within a broad frequency band is a central challenge in the search for wavelike dark matter. We explore quantum computing enhanced sensing based on the Grover search algorithm to address this problem and find that a long integration time stabilizes the accumulated sensing phase, reducing quantum signal processing (QSP) errors induced by dark matter fluctuations. We further propose alternating the signs of the QSP angles between oracle calls to suppress the coherent accumulation of the intrinsic QSP approximation errors during the search. Combining these strategies in a transmon-based benchmark, we obtain a projected sensitivity to axion dark matter beyond existing astrophysical limits. This opens access to substantial unexplored parameter space across the $10$-$100\,μ\mathrm{eV}$ mass range and offers an accelerated discovery channel for wavelike dark matter. With $10^6$ entangled sensing qubits, the projected sensitivity reaches the QCD axion band. Although illustrated with transmons, the protocol can be adapted to other experimental platforms for wavelike dark matter detection.
2611.14629.why: Grover-based quantum signal processing with alternating angles projects axion sensitivity beyond astrophysical limits on transmons.

2611.12548.title: Direct imaging of vortex lattices across fractional fillings in two-dimensional Josephson junction arrays
2611.12548.abstract: Josephson junction arrays are predicted to host a rich sequence of commensurate vortex lattices. However, direct imaging of these configurations remains limited, while transport measurements cannot resolve the underlying vortex arrangements or how order breaks down. Using scanning superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) microscopy, we resolve individual vortices and directly image this long-predicted hierarchy spanning filling factors $f$ = 1/8 to 1/2 in two-dimensional Au-Nb Josephson junction arrays, including several states with no discernible transport signatures. At $f$ = 1/4, two structurally distinct vortex orders with 4$\times$4 and 2$\times$4 unit cells coexist, consistent with their energetic degeneracy in the frustrated XY model. Away from commensurate filling, we resolve defect structures tied to the underlying vortex-lattice order: the $f$ = 1/2 checkerboard retains its order around isolated excess vortices and vacancies, whereas the $f$ = 1/3 staircase fragments into domains separated by domain walls. These results reveal how frustration, competing configurations, and defects shape the spatial coherence of commensurate vortex order in engineered superconducting lattices.
2611.12548.why: Scanning SQUID microscopy images commensurate vortex lattices from f=1/8 to 1/2 in Josephson junction arrays.

2611.16917.title: Enhancing optomechanical oscillation amplitude and frequency comb bandwidth by intensity-modulated driving
2611.16917.abstract: Self-sustained oscillations in optomechanical systems are attractive as compact, low-noise sources of GHz signals and optical frequency combs for integrated photonic circuits. For these applications, the achievable oscillation amplitude directly sets clock power and comb bandwidth. This work studies the maximum amplitude that can be reached through combinations of cavity backaction and modulated optical driving, with realistic resources. For an optically driven mechanical resonator, the oscillation amplitude saturates at a level set by the finite cavity bandwidth. We show that modulating the input intensity near the mechanical resonance frequency raises the achievable amplitude toward this limit at equal mean input power and cavity linewidth. We use a cycle-averaged energy-balance analysis to identify the added power that shifts the stable periodic orbit to larger amplitudes. Numerical integration of the full equations of motion confirms the enhancement across two decades of cooperativity and sideband-resolution ratios from 0.1 to 10. The relative increase in amplitude is largest near the self-oscillation threshold and in the sideband-unresolved regime, enabling threshold-free large-amplitude oscillation where backaction alone fails to do so. The enhanced amplitude leads to a larger modulation depth of the optical field, enabling broader frequency combs, with improved stability of the comb spacing. Intensity-modulated driving thus offers power-constrained platforms a simple open-loop route to larger mechanical amplitudes and enhanced comb bandwidth.
2611.16917.why: Intensity-modulated driving raises optomechanical self-oscillation amplitude toward the cavity-bandwidth limit.

2611.14474.title: Thin-film lithium niobate integrated photonics at 493 nm
2611.14474.abstract: Visible and near-ultraviolet light underpins applications from biophotonics to quantum computing, which demand fast control of optical amplitude and phase. Integrated photonics offers scalable control, yet most visible-wavelength platforms lack gigahertz-scale modulation. We demonstrate a thin-film lithium niobate platform at 493 nm integrating grating couplers, beamsplitters, ring resonators, and modulators. Segmented traveling-wave modulators achieve a half-wave voltage--length product of 450 mV$\cdot$cm, $>$20 dB extinction, and bandwidth beyond 50 GHz. Ring resonators show $2.9 \pm 0.2$ dB/cm propagation loss and quantify the platform's photorefractive response. This enables agile visible beam delivery for trapped-ion systems, although photorefraction and substrate uniformity remain key challenges to scaling.
2611.14474.why: Thin-film lithium niobate photonics at 493 nm with >50 GHz modulators for trapped-ion beam delivery.

2611.14398.title: Simulating closed- and open-system dynamics of Tavis--Cummings lattices on fault-tolerant quantum computers
2611.14398.abstract: Tavis--Cummings lattices couple cavities containing several emitters and host polaritonic many-body dynamics whose real-time correlations are costly to compute classically in two dimensions, especially when unequal emitter relaxation or dephasing rates break permutation symmetry. We analyze logical resources for fault-tolerant closed- and open-system simulation of an atom-resolved lattice with $L$ cavities, $N$ emitters per cavity, and photon cutoff $n\_{\max}$, including target observable estimation. Building on ladder-operator block encoding, we construct circuits for photon hopping and local light--matter exchange and combine them to encode the lattice Hamiltonian. By updating source and destination photon occupations in place, the hopping circuit eliminates the auxiliary $L\lceil\log_2(n\_{\max}+1)\rceil$-qubit photon register used by two-register implementations. Across three uniform-coefficient examples with $16$ to $256$ cavities, the controlled walk uses $4.75$--$8.11%$ fewer Toffoli gates than the paired two-register implementation under matched shared preparation, precision, control, and workspace conventions. For closed systems, we implement real-time evolution with generalized quantum signal processing and bound the cost of estimating retarded cavity spectral functions. For open systems with photon loss, emitter relaxation, and dephasing, we use a sampled first-order dilation and bound the runs and timesteps needed to estimate transient photon statistics such as $g^{(2)}(0)$. With state-preparation and measurement costs explicit, these estimates provide a reference for assessing fault-tolerant light--matter lattice simulation costs.
2611.14398.why: Fault-tolerant resource estimates for simulating Tavis-Cummings lattices, with an in-place photon-hopping circuit.

2611.13079.title: Quantum simulation of real-time bosonic dynamics with binary and unary position encodings on superconducting and trapped-ion processors
2611.13079.abstract: Simulating a bosonic degree of freedom on qubit hardware requires discretizing its position space, and the qubit encoding of the resulting lattice determines the circuits that realize its real-time dynamics. We compare binary and unary encodings of a position lattice on superconducting (IBM) and trapped-ion (IonQ) processors. Binary encoding applies the kinetic term through the quantum Fourier transform; unary encoding uses one qubit per site, single-qubit rotations for the potential and excitation-conserving exchange gates for the kinetic term. For a single degree of freedom the unary dynamics is a free-fermion problem, and its product formula compresses exactly into a nearest-neighbor circuit of fixed size. With about two hundred two-qubit gates, these circuits resolve tunneling in a symmetric double well on both processors, with the right-well probability falling from 0.97 to 0.06 on IBM and from 0.96 to 0.12 on IonQ, whereas binary product-formula circuits with several thousand two-qubit gates do not reproduce the transfer. Noiseless emulation indicates that this contrast reflects the compilation as well as the encoding: without the fixed-size optimization, a unary product formula that captures the transfer also requires several thousand two-qubit gates. Post-selection on the single-excitation subspace removes leakage, and because every energy eigenstate of the symmetric grid populates both wells equally, the measured population reversal bounds the coherence between energy eigenstates from below. Coupled-oscillator benchmarks, where inter-register interactions prevent this exact compression, show that the preferred encoding depends on the grid size and the evolution time.
2611.13079.why: Compares binary and unary bosonic encodings on IBM and IonQ, resolving double-well tunnelling.

2611.16071.title: Mapping the High-Field Response of Superconducting Nanowire Single-Photon Detectors
2611.16071.abstract: Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) are increasingly being integrated into cryogenic quantum-sensing platforms that operate in large magnetic fields. Here, the high-field limits of these measurements were probed by characterizing the dark count response of a NbTiN SNSPD at up to 14~T using in situ control of the detector orientation and benchmarking that performance against normal detector operation in smaller magnetic fields. The detector performance is strongly anisotropic: perpendicular magnetic fields rapidly reduce the usable bias-current range, whereas near-parallel alignment enables operation at substantially larger total fields, with a finite operating margin retained to 12~T and measurable dark-count response at the 14~T field limit. The angular dependence is governed predominantly by the perpendicular component of the magnetic field, consistent with vortex-mediated suppression of the superconducting current scale. The same field-dependent current scale also determines the electrical pulse amplitude, linking high-field detector operation directly to readout performance. These results establish a practical route for deploying SNSPDs in multi-tesla quantum-sensing and high-field cryogenic experiments.
2611.16071.why: Maps SNSPD dark-count response to 14 T; perpendicular field component governs operation.

2611.15757.title: Buffer-Gas-Assisted Fluorescence Spectroscopy of Molecular Ions
2611.15757.abstract: Sustained fluorescence detection of generic molecules has been challenging due to the lack of cycling transitions and limited photon budgets. We demonstrate a nondestructive method for continuous fluorescence of strongly rovibronically open molecular ions, $^{232}$ThF$^+$. Effective quasi-cycling transitions are established by room-temperature buffer-gas collisions, which replenish the population back to the laser-addressed states. In situ images and rotationally resolved spectra are obtained without optical repumping or auxiliary atomic readout ions. Combined with low-background spectroscopic detection, this approach achieves a signal-to-noise ratio of approximately 6 in a 1 s exposure on the P(1) line of $^{232}$ThF$^+$, despite a thermal population of only approximately 0.17% in the addressed state at room temperature. The ability to repeatedly interrogate trapped ions is particularly promising for scarce molecular samples, broadband spectroscopic searches, and in situ monitoring of molecular reactions.
2611.15757.why: Buffer-gas collisions give quasi-cycling fluorescence from trapped ThF+ ions.

2611.14291.title: Nonreciprocal Josephson Dynamics of a $\mathcal{PT}$-Symmetric Atomtronic SQUID
2611.14291.abstract: We investigate non-Hermitian Josephson dynamics in an atomtronic quantum interference device (AQUID), formed by a ring Bose Einstein condensate with balanced atomic gain and loss regions and two moving optical barriers. The balanced gain and loss profile establishes a parity time symmetric potential while breaking spatial inversion symmetry, providing the essential ingredients for nonreciprocal Josephson transport. The dynamics are monitored nondestructively through the phase quadrature spectrum of an optomechanical cavity driven by Laguerre Gaussian beams coupled to the condensate. We demonstrate that increasing the local gain and loss strength softens the parity time symmetric collective mode towards an exceptional point, as verified by Bogoliubov de Gennes analysis. The associated coherent population exchange produces an additional characteristic splitting in the cavity output spectrum. For linearly translating barriers, non-Hermiticity provides an additional control parameter for tuning the critical current. When the barriers undergo simultaneous translation and rotation, the rotation induced phase modifies the interference between counter propagating currents, offering further control over the nonreciprocal response. Under periodic barrier modulation, we find more pronounced Shapiro steps in the current voltage characteristics due to the intrinsic parity time symmetric collective mode. Finally, we propose an alternative Hermitian realization using a tilted optical lattice, providing an experimentally accessible route to engineering biased transport and population transfer. Our results establish parity time symmetric atomtronic SQUIDs as a versatile platform for controlling nonreciprocal Josephson transport and collective excitations in driven quantum fluids.
2611.14291.why: PT-symmetric atomtronic SQUID shows nonreciprocal Josephson dynamics read out optomechanically.

2611.10988.title: Deterministically fabricated C-band single-photon sources based on quantum dot circular Bragg grating cavities
2611.10988.abstract: Telecom-wavelength quantum light sources are essential components for scalable fiber-based quantum networks, where on-demand emission of single photons is required for high secret key rates. Here, we demonstrate the deterministic integration of metal-organic vapor-phase epitaxy (MOVPE)-grown C-band InAs/InP quantum dots into circular Bragg grating resonators. The integrated emitters exhibit a radiative lifetime of $T_1 = (1400 \pm 50)~\mathrm{ps}$ and a spectral linewidth of $ΔE_{\mathrm{FWHM}} = (41.0 \pm 4.0)~μ\mathrm{eV}$. Under non-resonant excitation, we measure a post-selected single-photon purity of $(0.95 \pm 0.02)$ and a raw two-photon interference visibility of $V_{12\mathrm{ns}} = (35 \pm 2)\%$, which increases to $(70 \pm 18)\%$ under temporal post-selection. We discuss strategies to improve photon indistinguishability, including radiative-rate engineering, charge stabilization, and more selective excitation. Our results combine MOVPE growth, deterministic device integration, and telecom C-band emission, providing a route toward scalable semiconductor quantum light sources for fiber-based quantum networks.
2611.10988.why: C-band quantum dots in circular Bragg gratings with 0.95 purity and 35% raw HOM visibility.

2611.11356.title: What an Observer Reads off a Holographic Screen
2611.11356.abstract: What does an observer read off a holographic screen that is an array of qubits rather than a surface? In the generalized holographic principle the interaction between two separable systems acts on such a screen as a weighted sum, up to an overall prefactor, of commuting observables with values plus and minus one. When the weights are nonnegative and the prefactor is one and the joint eigenspaces are lines, everything a probe reads off the spectrum depends only on the list of weights, which we call the profile. On the screen with equal weights summing to one the running dimension read by a diffusion probe falls short of two at unit time by at most twice the reciprocal of the number of qubits; a geometric profile gives instead, through its level count, a plateau of any positive height. An observer correlates sets of qubits; its readout carries a profile at a given weighting when the levels it reads, counted with multiplicity, are those of a screen with one weight per set. We prove that a readout carries a profile at every weighting exactly when the distinct nonzero traces of its qubits are linearly independent over the field with two elements, the trace of a qubit being the list of sets that contain it; such a readout is a partition of the qubits it covers up to an invertible recoding, and a dependent one carries a profile only on finitely many proper linear subspaces of weightings. Refining a grouping without end builds a tower whose boundary is a profinite set and hence a condensed set, on which a strictly positive compatible profile separates the locally constant functions by a distance. Applications certify probabilistic and strong contextuality and give the leading shortfall of the distance between the poles of the fuzzy sphere; in a model of monogamous entanglement the pairs that weight-one threads representing operational ER=EPR can occupy at once are exactly the partial matchings.
2611.11356.why: Defines spectral 'profiles' an observer reads from a qubit holographic screen and bounds the diffusion dimension.

eli5.plain: What a probe can learn from an array of qubits interacting as a holographic screen.
eli5.how: Interactions written as weighted sums of commuting ±1 observables; spectra depend only on the weights.
eli5.matters: Speculative link between observers and emergent geometry.
eli5.caveat: Highly formal; physical reading is thin.

2611.14611.title: Probing Krylov Dynamics in Driven Many-Body Systems
2611.14611.abstract: Krylov complexity has become a central probe of operator growth, scrambling, and quantum chaos. Yet, a basic fact hinders its experimental study: laboratory quantum systems are routinely driven in time, whereas the Krylov construction assumes a fixed generator and breaks down once the Hamiltonian varies. Here, we solve the time-dependent many-body Krylov problem exactly and in closed form for scale- and rotation-invariant systems realized in current quantum-simulation and control platforms. We find exact relations that map the driven dynamics onto mutually orthogonal Krylov subspaces and yield a closed-form spread complexity, determined solely by the spectral properties of the initial Hamiltonian and the driving schedule. The construction extends to Liouville space and solves the time-dependent density-matrix Krylov problem, which makes the Krylov dynamics of initial thermal states experimentally accessible. In scale-invariant quantum gases, such as the driven Lieb-Liniger model, the Tonks-Girardeau gas, and the Calogero-Sutherland model, the complexity is set by the width of the atomic cloud and its rate of change, directly accessible via in situ and time-of-flight imaging. In rotation-invariant spin systems such as the Haldane-Shastry and central-spin models, it is governed by collective spin precession that can be probed and read out in trapped-ion, cavity-QED, and circuit-QED platforms.
2611.14611.why: Closed-form time-dependent Krylov complexity for scale-invariant driven systems.

2611.14231.title: From Growth to Devices: Oxygen-Controlled Superconductivity in BSCCO Thin Films
2611.14231.abstract: Realizing device-compatible high-$T_c$ superconductors requires simultaneous control of oxygen stoichiometry and tolerance to nanofabrication. Here, we investigate sputtered Bi$_2$Sr$_2$Ca$_{n-1}$Cu$_n$O$_{2n+4+δ}$ (BSCCO) thin films and establish a direct link between annealing conditions, oxygen incorporation, and superconducting transport. By independently varying the annealing temperature and duration, we identify an optimal annealing condition of $860\,^{\circ}$C for 3\,h, which yields the highest superconducting transition temperature and the narrowest transition among the investigated samples. X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, and X-ray photoemission spectroscopy reveal a non-monotonic evolution of lattice oxygen, which governs hole doping in the CuO$_2$ planes and produces the characteristic dome-like dependence of $T_c$ on doping concentration. We further translate these optimized films into micro-devices to assess fabrication-induced effects, via micro-bridges as well as a planar Josephson junction. We demonstrate devices fabricated via both lift-off and focused ion beam (FIB) patterning methods -- proving the fabrication compatibility of these films. Importantly, we demonstrate their air-stability for extended periods of time (2 months). The combined insights offer practical guidelines for integrating cuprate thin films into superconducting electronics and quantum device architectures.
2611.14231.why: Annealing recipe optimizes oxygen doping and Tc in sputtered BSCCO films.

2611.16519.title: Effect of atomic interactions on quantum communication protocols
2611.16519.abstract: We develop a first-principles framework for analyzing photonic quantum communication in an atomic medium. Starting from a real-space quantization of the electromagnetic field coupled to an ensemble of two-level atoms, we derive an effective model for polarization-encoded single-photon states. We apply this framework to superdense coding to study communication efficiency and to the BB84 quantum key distribution protocol for communication security. For superdense coding, we evaluate the protocol capacity of the fixed Bell-state alphabet under erasure, dephasing, and depolarizing channels and show that it decreases monotonically with increasing atom-field coupling. For BB84, we formulate a modified protocol that discards erasure outcomes and uses the microscopic model to estimate the intrinsic loss rate. We derive the corresponding asymptotic key rate and show that it decreases monotonically with coupling strength and vanishes beyond a finite critical coupling.
2611.16519.why: Atomic-medium model shows superdense coding and BB84 rates fall with atom-field coupling.

2611.15516.title: Feedback Control and Neural-Network-Based Prediction of Quantum Entanglement in Fano-mirror cavity optomechanics
2611.15516.abstract: Quantum entanglement involving the centre-of-mass motion of macroscopic-scale objects plays an essential role in both fundamental science and emerging quantum technologies, yet generating and verifying such macroscopic nonclassical states remain formidable challenges. Here, we report a theoretical scheme to effectively generate, manipulate, and predict bipartite optomechanical entanglement based on a Fano-mirror cavity optomechanical system with a coherent feedback loop, where the cavity and Fano optical modes couple through coherent and dissipative interactions. We show that the Fano mirror forms a closed tripartite interaction loop with the cavity and mechanical modes, whereby the quantum interference between direct and indirect interaction pathways substantially enhances the cavity-mechanical entanglement and gives rise to a robust Fano-mechanical entanglement. More importantly, we find that coherent feedback combined with an appropriate optical frequency mismatch can further enhance the entanglement, and a trained supervised feedforward neural network can be used to predict the entanglement magnitude from the readily measurable optical signals, relaxing the requirement of full quantum-state tomography. Our work, establishing an all-optical and experimentally feasible approach to generate, manipulate, and characterize the macroscopic optomechanical entanglement, holds great potential for applications in quantum information processing.
2611.15516.why: Fano-mirror optomechanics with feedback enhances entanglement; neural network predicts it.

2611.14044.title: CV-TF-QKD
2611.14044.abstract: We introduce a continuous-variable version of twin-field quantum key distribution, using independent Gaussian-modulated coherent states and an untrusted single-photon relay. Full-record reconciliation and a binary phase-disclosure protocol achieve nearly equal asymptotic key rates against collective attacks. At fixed weak input-referred excess noise per arm, both rates per relay use scale as $\sqrtη$, where $η$ is the end-to-end transmissivity. For phase disclosure, we establish composable security against general coherent attacks using a bounded test of preparation intensities and sign-parity complementarity. For specified apparatus parameters, finite-key calculations incorporating detector inefficiency, dark counts, phase fluctuations, and reference overhead predict rates exceeding the pure-loss and matched thermal-loss repeaterless bounds. These results extend the twin-field advantage to Gaussian-modulated continuous-variable quantum cryptography.
2611.14044.why: Continuous-variable twin-field QKD with √η key-rate scaling and composable security.

2611.10442.title: Transverse quasiparticle heat transport in p-wave magnetic Josephson junctions
2611.10442.abstract: We study transverse heat currents carried by Bogoliubov quasiparticles in $p$-wave magnetic Josephson junctions under a longitudinal temperature bias. We find that such a junction supports a transverse spin heat current while the net transverse heat current vanishes. This effect stems from the $p$-wave magnetism, which shifts the two spin sectors oppositely in transverse momentum space and thereby causes them to carry opposite heat currents. A weak Zeeman field lifts the compensation between the two spin-sector contributions, thereby generating a finite net transverse heat current. The directions of both currents can be switched by reversing the sign of the $p$-wave magnetic splitting or tuning the superconducting phase difference, while both currents vanish in the absence of $p$-wave magnetism. These findings highlight $p$-wave magnetic Josephson junctions as a versatile platform for switchable transverse heat transport and controllable spin caloritronics.
2611.10442.why: p-wave magnetic Josephson junctions carry a transverse spin heat current switchable by phase.

2611.16607.title: Beauty and charm jet identification with end-to-end training on a superconducting quantum processor
2611.16607.abstract: The identification of heavy-flavor jets, i.e. collimated streams of particles originating from the fragmentation of beauty and charm quarks produced in proton-proton collisions, represents one of the most challenging classification tasks in measurements at Large Hadron Collider experiments. In recent years, advanced machine learning techniques have been successfully employed to address this problem, while quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising alternative approach. However, the high dimensionality of the problem, typically involving hundreds of observables, raises an open question: whether the current generation of quantum computers, characterized by limited qubit count, can effectively tackle such complex tasks. In this work, a variational quantum circuit for the classification of b- and c-jets at the LHCb experiment is implemented on a 5-qubit superconducting quantum computer manufactured by IQM and installed at the Politecnico di Torino. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a quantum algorithm for jet identification using simulated data from an LHC experiment in which all stages of the machine-learning workflow, including training and testing, are performed on real quantum hardware. The results demonstrate that the impact of hardware-induced quantum noise does not significantly degrade the performance. A framework for the evaluation of the training time on the quantum hardware and for the circuit optimization is also proposed. These findings pave the way for future applications on larger quantum devices based on superconducting qubits, featuring a larger number of qubits enabling the encoding of information beyond the reach of classical simulation and providing a step toward investigating whether quantum advantage may eventually be achievable in high-energy physics classification tasks.
2611.16607.why: Five-qubit variational classifier for b/c jets at LHCb, trained end-to-end on hardware.

2611.17988.title: A Concise Introduction to Quantum Electromagnetics
2611.17988.abstract: This book introduces quantum electromagnetics to readers trained in classical electromagnetics, without assuming a systematic background in quantum mechanics. The central question is when classical descriptions suffice, and when the quantum states of matter or the field must be retained explicitly. Starting from familiar electromagnetic modes and material response, the discussion develops atomic dynamics, field quantization, and the interaction of quantized fields with quantum matter. Particular attention is given to how mode profiles, Green functions, and scattering matrices obtained from classical electromagnetic calculations enter quantum models. Atomic coherence, photon statistics, spontaneous emission, and cavity coupling are developed through derivations that identify the physical assumptions and limits of each description. Examples drawn from atomic clocks, Rydberg-atom receivers, and single-photon devices connect these concepts to excitation, propagation, and measurement in practical systems. Loss and noise are included in relating internal dynamics to measured signals and correlations. The final discussion examines how sensitivity and claims of quantum advantage depend on bandwidth, measurement resources, and the classical reference used for comparison. The aim is to help readers choose an appropriate model, carry out the calculation, and understand what its predictions mean for an electromagnetic measurement.
2611.17988.why: Textbook introducing quantum electromagnetics to classical EM engineers.

2611.18136.title: Quantum tomography of Higgsstrahlung: Higgs boson self-coupling and $Z$ boson anomalous couplings
2611.18136.abstract: The Higgs boson self-coupling enters the Higgsstrahlung process $e^+e^-\to ZH$ at one loop. The three diagrams that carry it project onto two Lorentz structures: the tree-level one, which rescales the rate, and that of the CP-even anomalous coupling $b_Z$, which changes the polarization of the final-state $Z$ boson. To assess how well quantum state tomography constrains the $hZZ$ anomalous couplings and the trilinear coupling at FCC-ee, we compute the helicity density matrix of the $Z$ boson, for an effective vertex that also includes a CP-odd anomalous coupling $\tilde b_Z$, together with its complete one-loop correction in the Standard Model. With these corrections and no other new physics in the effective vertex, quantum state tomography determines $κ_λ$ to $\pm 3.9$, or $\pm 2.9$ with the full angular information, independently of the rate and of the normalization of the vertex, and not far from the limit $δκ_λ\simeq 1$ set by the quantum Fisher information. Without assumptions on the new physics, quantum tomography directly bounds the anomalous couplings at the $10^{-3}$ level, improving on the existing projections. The density matrix also characterizes the $Z$ boson as a qutrit. At $365$ GeV its state in the central region is pure enough to violate the Klyachko--Can--Binicioğlu--Shumovsky contextuality inequality, $\mathbb{CNTXT}_5 = 2.06$ at $θ= π/2$ against the non-contextual bound $2$. We also quantify the purity and the amount of magic of the $Z$ boson state, using the mana, the stabilizer Rényi entropy and the robustness of magic for the latter. At fixed angle, purity, contextuality and magic are robust against anomalous couplings of the size probed by the tomography. The inclusive state, instead, is neither contextual in this test nor magic in the helicity basis.
2611.18136.why: Z-boson helicity tomography at FCC-ee constrains the Higgs self-coupling to ±2.9.

2611.11754.title: Advantage Distillation in Paired-State Quantum Key Distribution
2611.11754.abstract: We investigate advantage distillation for paired-state Loop-Back quantum key distribution, with a fixed optical station serving a lightweight portable terminal. Alice prepares two polarization-encoded pulses, Bob selects and applies a polarization filter to each pulse, and Alice infers his selections from the returned detection pattern. The proposed advantage-distillation step selects consistent blocks of three two-bit records using two independent public parity checks on a minimal connected graph. The closing edge of a parity polygon is shown to be redundant: any spanning tree of the same vertices has the same acceptance set. We derive exact acceptance probabilities, residual-error laws, and retention rates. Under independent bit errors, the three-record filter reduces the leading error term from e to e^2, while its cost in discarded records and public information is accounted for explicitly. A modular security theorem bounds the additional guessing advantage available to an adversary after syndrome disclosure and block acceptance, including arbitrary quantum side information. We also evaluate a specified single-photon passive-tap optical channel, obtaining a positive conditional entropy bound and exact accepted-block security quantities. This parity-based advantage-distillation step detects discrepancies by postselection; it does not correct individual errors and is intended to precede conventional reconciliation. The architecture suggests two further directions: hybrid filtering and reconciliation, and key establishment between portable users accessing a shared quantum station.
2611.11754.why: Advantage distillation for paired-state loop-back QKD reduces error from e to e².

2611.11568.title: Spin entanglement in $pp$ and $pA$ collisions: high-energy TMD effects and fragmentation probes
2611.11568.abstract: Spin-spin correlations of a quark-antiquark pair produced in proton-proton or proton-Ion collisions are investigated in $k_T$-factorization within the shockwave formalism. We construct the full spin-density matrix of both inclusive and diffractive channels in the limit in which the two quarks are back-to-back. In the inclusive channel, due to linearly polarized gluons, we show that a $\cos (2 φ)$-modulation of the concurrence, stabilizer Rényi entropy, and quantum discord emerges and depends on the interplay between six small-$x$ gluon TMDs. The modulation is predicted to be maximally strong and independent of the transverse momentum imbalance, $q$, from a dilute (BFKL) perspective, while it is considerably suppressed by saturation effects. In diffraction, we observe that the pair is always entangled and exhibits the same properties found in diffractive DIS. We explain how these properties follow directly from the exclusive and eikonal nature of the Pomeron exchange. We trace this behavior to a spin-density matrix of rank at most two with maximally mixed marginals. For this class of states, entanglement and Bell nonlocality coincide even when the state is mixed, while the explicit form of the light-front helicity amplitudes ensures that both persist in the whole phase space. We suggest accessing the spin correlations in unpolarized hadron collisions through the Collins and dihadron fragmentation functions. We point out that, in inclusive production, for massless quarks, suitably chosen double-Collins asymmetries provide promising entanglement witnesses.
2611.11568.why: Spin entanglement of quark pairs in pp and pA collisions shows cos2φ modulation from gluon TMDs.

2611.10183.title: Current-voltage characteristics of layered cuprate superconductors with intrinsic Josephson junctions
2611.10183.abstract: A brief review of the results for the current-voltage characteristics study in highly anisotropic cuprate superconductors is presented, considering the existence of the intrinsic Josephson effect in multilayer HTSC compounds. We analyzed the observations of multi-branch current-voltage characteristics for current in the c-direction both for the hole-doped and electron-doped cuprate SCs wich conveniently viewed as a strack of intrinsic Josephson junctions, where the CuO2 layers serve as superconducting plates and the buffer layers as dielectric interlayers. It was shown that the tunneling characteristics of intrinsic Josephson junctions in optimally doped p- and n-type cuprates indicate a predominantly d-wave symmetry of the order parameter, demonstrating high conductivity in the subgap regime: U < 2delta/e. The analysis carried out confirms the theoretically predicted power-law dependences U ~ I^gamma with gamma = (0.33 - 0.50) in the hole-doped Bi- and Tl-compounds, which is typical for SCs with monotonic dx^2-y^2 - wave symmetry of the order parameter and with gamma = (0.70 - 0.76) for electron-doped SCs with a non-monotonic d-wave symmetry within the framework of the two-band/two-gap model.
2611.10183.why: Brief review of intrinsic Josephson current-voltage characteristics in cuprates.

2611.17588.title: Deep, label-free, volumetric lifetime microscopy via low-noise, single pulse sampling
2611.17588.abstract: Fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM) provides label-free metabolic contrast, but conventional time-correlated single-photon counting requires thousands of excitation pulses per pixel to avoid pile-up distortion, limiting imaging speed and increasing motion artifacts and photodamage. Here, we develop single-pulse analog sampling that combines sub-photoelectron read noise with a jitter-immune, frequency-domain estimator for accurate lifetime measurement at low photon counts. Single low-flux traces achieve a photon economy of $F < 1.5$ at 100--150 detected photons, enabling accurate lifetime estimation from a single excitation pulse in label-free, volumetric samples. In in vivo zebrafish eyes, single-shot acquisition recovered the lifetime content of 20-pulse averaging at one-twentieth the exposure, resolving endogenous lipofuscin heterogeneity. In intact mouse kidney, scattering and reduced photon throughput impaired lifetime contrast; this was mitigated by lightweight denoisers that enabled label-free lifetime imaging to 200 micron depth at one pulse per pixel. These results establish single-shot FLIM as a route to deeper, faster, motion-tolerant, low-photodamage lifetime imaging.
2611.17588.why: Single-pulse analog sampling enables fluorescence lifetime imaging from one excitation pulse.

2611.16774.title: Inter-city 18.9 km free-space QKD over a dense urban corridor
2611.16774.abstract: Terrestrial free-space quantum key distribution (QKD) provides a flexible complement to fiber-based networks, but its deployment over long horizontal paths in dense metropolitan environments remains challenging, as atmospheric turbulence, demanding pointing and tracking requirements, and operational constraints can substantially increase system complexity. We experimentally demonstrate the operation of a decoy-state BB84 system over an 18.9~km free-space link across a densely populated urban area in the metropolitan region of Barcelona using an aviation-compliant optical architecture. The system operates at 785~nm using room-temperature single-photon detectors and requires no adaptive optics at the receiver. The modular QKD transmitter, based on a deployment-oriented design, is interfaced with a versatile free-space optical terminal and an independent GPS-disciplined synchronization architecture, facilitating its integration into heterogeneous optical infrastructures. We present the transmitter performance and optical-link characteristics, together with a 40-minute field test characterized by an average channel attenuation of approximately 19~dB and a mean QBER of 1.31\%. From the measured channel parameters, we estimate an average finite-size secret key rate exceeding 11~kbit/s. These results demonstrate the feasibility of inter-city free-space QKD over dense urban areas using a comparatively simple architecture.
2611.16774.why: Decoy-state BB84 over 18.9 km urban free-space link without adaptive optics.

2611.16717.title: Optical fiber shape sensing using picosecond spatiotemporal single-photon reflectometry
2611.16717.abstract: Inferring the three-dimensional configuration of a flexible optical fiber from a single accessible end remains a fundamental challenge in photonic sensing. Existing approaches typically require specialised multicore fibers, coherent interferometry, or distributed spectral encoding. Here, we demonstrate a fundamentally different sensing paradigm in which fiber geometry is reconstructed from the spatiotemporal dynamics of returning single photons. Using a laser-engineered multimode fiber interrogated by a time-resolved 32x32 single-photon avalanche diode array, we show that fiber deformation imprints unique signatures onto the distribution and arrival time of back-reflected photons. We map these high-dimensional photon-return states onto a low-dimensional geometric manifold, enabling continuous bend-angle estimation and reconstruction of previously unseen two- and three-dimensional shapes from measurements acquired entirely at the proximal fiber end. Measurements show a median pixel-wise signal-to-noise ratio of approximately 26 dB and below 1% repeatability variation. Our results establish multimode single-photon dynamics as an information-rich channel for distributed geometric sensing, introducing a new framework for single-ended fiber shape reconstruction and minimally invasive photonic navigation.
2611.16717.why: Reconstructs fiber shape from time-resolved single-photon back-reflections on a SPAD array.

2611.05355.title: Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits
2611.05355.abstract: When a language model answers, we can usually only estimate why. We build a transformer in which every nonlinearity is a quadratic detection - an interference, a balanced reading or a camera - and the output is a Born probability: attention |<q|k>|^2, the form of the Born rule, normalised per row, a measured product for the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout; between detections, classical control rescales and re-encodes. With its denominators held at the input, each class probability is a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so its integrated-gradient evidence is computed by a finite quadrature with no quadrature error: the words' contributions sum to the class probability above its no-information share to 10^-13. On e-SNLI natural language inference it reaches 77.45 +- 0.91 % accuracy, level with a same-size softmax transformer (76.62 +- 0.36 %) and an order-free bag of embeddings (77.79 %). Exactness buys the sum, not the best ranking. Deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 44 % of pairs, of the 53 % some deletion changes, against 31-32 % for the softmax model's integrated gradients; the model's own gradient x input does as well (43 %), as does a bag of embeddings' (43 %, seed 0), and leave-one-out does better. Holding the denominators helps the low end: the five words ranked last change the answer in 1 %, against 6 % free. The same weights compile exactly to simulated optoelectronics, and their attention to qubits. On ibm_kingston, reading only the attention, the device gave the model's answers in all three Hadamard-test runs (the two shortest pairs and one without its deciding word) and both compute-uncompute runs (one circuit per overlap); uniform attention answers otherwise on two of the three inputs. With the device's row sums the evidence correlated with the exact one at 0.997 and 0.962 by Hadamard tests; with compute-uncompute, 0.971 and 0.48.
2611.05355.why: Transformer with Born-rule attention gives exact word attributions at softmax-level accuracy.

2611.11590.title: Comments on: "Optimized thermal control of a dual-wavelength-resonant nonlinear cavity"
2611.11590.abstract: This comment addresses the publication [Appl. Opt. 65, 7090 (2026)] which targets an alleged ``optimization'' of a patented invention conceived by the author. The invention had introduced a multi-temperature management scheme for a dual-wavelength-resonant nonlinear cavity that optimized the crystal temperature around the beam waist for phase-matching, while utilizing independently adjustable temperatures in other regions of the same crystal to simultaneously satisfy the double-resonance condition. A foundational form of this invention was initially utilized by co-author H. Vahlbruch without the author's prior knowledge during the construction of the squeezed-light laser for the Virgo gravitational wave detector. In their publication, the three authors now propose a variant that reduces the maximum achievable temperature differential. Here, I demonstrate that this approach does not constitute an optimization but, on the contrary, represents a regression that dismantles the invention. In general, a high-quality implementation of this invention fundamentally depends on maximizing the achievable temperature differential. Only then can the problematic phase differences---introduced by dielectric coatings, Gouy phase shifts, and suboptimal poling lengths at the crystal facets---be effectively compensated for, particularly in short crystals. If desired, smaller temperature differences can always be selected dynamically anyway.
2611.11590.why: Comment disputing novelty of a dual-resonant cavity thermal-control scheme.

2611.13815.title: Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM): A Unified Learning-Based Framework for Noise Resilience in Quantum Machine Learning
2611.13815.abstract: Error mitigation stands between variational quantum algorithms and useful results on today's noisy hardware, yet in practice a mitigation method is usually chosen once, by hand, and applied unchanged for the life of an experiment. This is a poor fit for quantum machine learning (QML), where the circuit and the noise drift as training proceeds, so the best strategy in one regime is often wrong in another. We present a generalized form of Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM), which treats the choice of mitigation technique as an online decision made from an algorithm's own feedback. A single contextual-bandit controller observes signals any variational algorithm already produces, such as fidelity, entropy, reward or loss, and gradient behavior, and selects among Zero-Noise Extrapolation, Probabilistic Error Cancellation, Measurement Error Mitigation, Dynamical Decoupling, and circuit optimization per step. Because it depends only on this shared feedback interface, the framework applies unchanged across supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and hybrid quantum-classical learning. Evaluated on five paradigms across 80 algorithm-and-noise conditions, adaptive selection reaches 95.5% of an oracle that always picks the best technique and significantly outperforms all six fixed strategies (Friedman $χ^{2}=92.18$, $p\approx1.1\times10^{-17}$; pairwise Wilcoxon $p<4\times10^{-6}$). The learned policy is noise-aware: its favored technique shifts as depolarizing and readout error rise. On noise models from eight real IBM devices, APGEM tracks the oracle almost exactly (99.9% of oracle utility) at a flat cost of roughly $1.3\times10^{4}$ shots from three to eight qubits.
2611.13815.why: Contextual-bandit controller picks error-mitigation methods on the fly for QML.
